name: AI for School and Educational Leaders 8: Final Project and Capstone
objectives: Given a challenge in your school, write a student-centered problem statement with evidence, saying what is wrong, for whom and how much, and whether AI is the right answer
Given your problem, set a small pilot scope and choose a tool that passes vendor review, naming who, what changes and how long, with the tool chosen after the scope

Before the pilot starts, run a privacy and equity check with a guard and an owner for each risk, covering FERPA, COPPA if students are under 13, accessibility and access, signed off by the privacy officer
For the staff in the pilot, plan hands-on training, rules and support, with a 60-minute training agenda, a named contact and the notes teachers will keep
For families of students in the pilot, write an honest family letter and a five-question FAQ, under one page, checked by a parent or family liaison, with translations checked by qualified speakers

For your full pilot plan, set three to five success measures with a baseline and a go, adjust or stop rule, and present the plan, in ten minutes, with the rule written before the start and the questions and answers recorded

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Start with a student-centered problem
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Define the problem your pilot will solve, with evidence and the students it serves.
This lesson builds toward: Given a challenge in your school, you will write a student-centered problem statement with evidence, saying what is wrong, for whom and how much, and whether AI is the right answer.
Strong pilots start with a problem, not a product. Ask: what is getting in the way of student learning or wellbeing, or of teachers' time with students? Examples: teachers spend hours each week on family translations; students in grade 9 algebra need more practice with feedback; new teachers struggle to differentiate.
Gather evidence: data you already have (with privacy protections), teacher and student surveys, and conversations. Write the problem in one sentence with who is affected and how much: "Our 9th-grade algebra teachers report under 10 minutes a week per student for individual feedback, and 40 percent of students failed the first unit test."
Then ask whether AI is the right answer at all. Sometimes a schedule change, a template or more staff time solves it better. If AI is a fit, say exactly what it will do.
Step by step:
- List problems that block learning, wellbeing or teacher time.
- Gather evidence: data, surveys, conversations.
- Write the problem in one sentence: who, what, how much.
- Ask whether AI is the right answer.
- If yes, say exactly what AI will do.
Words to know:
- Problem statement: one sentence that says what is wrong, for whom, and how much.
- Evidence: data and observations that show a problem is real.
Try it now: Write your problem statement in one sentence with evidence, and one sentence on exactly what AI would do about it, or why something else would work better.
You can now define a student-centered problem with evidence before choosing any AI tool.

check.q: What does a problem statement say?
options: Which AI tool you want to buy
What is wrong, for whom, and how much
How much the pilot will cost
Who will present the plan
check.why: A clear problem statement keeps the pilot focused on students, not on a tool.

check.q: A vendor offers your school a free AI tool. What would you do first?
options: Start using it, since it is free
Pick a problem it might solve later
Define the student problem and ask whether AI is the right answer at all
Ask students to try it at home
check.why: Strong pilots start from a student-centered problem, not a tool.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scoping the pilot and choosing the tool
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set a small, clear pilot scope and choose a tool that passes vendor review.
This lesson builds toward: Given your problem, you will set a small pilot scope and choose a tool that passes vendor review, naming who, what changes and how long, with the tool chosen after the scope.
Keep it small: a few teachers or one grade or course, for six to twelve weeks. A small pilot is easier to support, measure and stop if needed. Write who takes part, what they will do differently, and when.
Choose the tool last. Prefer tools already approved in your district, or ones that pass the vendor review from course 7 (the Model Terms of Service checklist plus AI questions about accuracy, bias, accessibility and teacher override). Check the tool's age rules if students will use it.
Consider funding. The Department of Education's July 2025 Dear Colleague Letter, as reported by K-12 Dive, says existing federal grant funds may support AI for high-quality curriculum tools, high-impact tutoring, and college and career pathway advising, if legal requirements are met. Check the letter on ed.gov and with your federal programs office before planning on any funds.
Step by step:
- Choose a small group and six to twelve weeks.
- Write who, what changes, and when.
- Prefer approved tools; otherwise run the vendor review.
- Check age rules if students use it.
- Check funding with your federal programs office.
Words to know:
- Scope: the size and limits of a project: who, what and how long.
- Federal programs office: the district office that manages federal grants like Title I.
Official sources:
- K-12 Dive: Education Department issues AI priorities (July 2025)
- Privacy and Education Technology: Model Terms of Service checklist
Try it now: Write your pilot scope (who, what changes, how long) and name the tool, with its approval status or the vendor review you ran.
You can now scope a small AI pilot and choose a tool that has been properly reviewed.

check.q: What is a good pilot scope?
options: Every school in the district for three years
A few teachers in one course for six to twelve weeks
One student for one day
No set length
check.why: A small, clear scope lets you learn quickly and limit risk.

check.q: The tool you want is not yet approved by the district. What do you do?
options: Run the vendor review before the pilot
Use it anyway for a short pilot
Ask teachers to buy it themselves
Choose a tool at random
check.why: Tools must pass vendor review before students or staff use them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The privacy and equity check
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run a privacy and equity check on your pilot before it starts.
This lesson builds toward: Before the pilot starts, you will run a privacy and equity check with a guard and an owner for each risk, covering FERPA, COPPA if students are under 13, accessibility and access, signed off by the privacy officer.
Privacy: list exactly what student data the pilot uses and where it goes. Under FERPA, sharing personally identifiable information from education records with a vendor generally needs consent unless an exception applies, such as a vendor acting as a school official under the school's direct control with limits on re-sharing. If students are under 13, COPPA applies; school consent works only for school use with no other commercial purpose. Get your privacy officer's sign-off.
Equity: who might be left out or harmed? Check access (devices, internet, accessibility for students with disabilities, languages for families), whether results could differ by student group, and whether any AI output could affect grades, placement or discipline; if so, add human review.
Write the check on one page with each risk, the guard and the owner. A pilot that has not passed this check is not ready to start.
Step by step:
- List the student data, where it goes and why.
- Check FERPA, and COPPA if students are under 13.
- Get the privacy officer's sign-off.
- Check access, accessibility, languages and group differences.
- Write each risk with its guard and owner.
Words to know:
- Sign-off: formal approval from the person responsible.
- Accessibility: whether people with disabilities can fully use a tool.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: Write your one-page privacy and equity check with at least three privacy risks and three equity risks, each with a guard and an owner.
You can now check an AI pilot for privacy and equity risks before it starts.

check.q: Which is an equity question for a pilot?
options: Is the tool popular?
Is the tool the newest?
Does the tool have a nice design?
Can students with disabilities fully use the tool?
check.why: Accessibility and access are part of the equity check.

check.q: Your privacy and equity check is not finished, but the start date is tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Start anyway and finish the check later
Delay the start until the check is done and signed off
Skip the equity part
Start with only half the students
check.why: A pilot that has not passed the privacy and equity check is not ready to start.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Preparing staff
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan the training and support pilot staff need.
This lesson builds toward: For the staff in the pilot, you will plan hands-on training, rules and support, with a 60-minute training agenda, a named contact and the notes teachers will keep.
Teachers in the pilot need more than a login. Plan three things. Skills: how to use the tool well, the prompts or settings that work, and how to check its output. Rules: privacy, the AI use levels for students, and what to do when something goes wrong. Support: a named contact, a weekly check-in, and time to try things.
Make training hands-on. Teachers should use the tool on their own real (non-private) materials during the session, not watch a demo. Pair early adopters with cautious colleagues.
Ask pilot teachers to keep short notes: time spent, what worked, what failed, student reactions. Their notes are part of your evidence and will shape the decision at the end.
Step by step:
- Plan skills: use, prompts, checking output.
- Plan rules: privacy, student use levels, incidents.
- Plan support: contact, weekly check-in, time.
- Make sessions hands-on with real materials.
- Ask teachers to keep short notes.
Words to know:
- Professional development (PD): training and learning for teachers and staff.
- Early adopter: someone who tries new tools early and can help others.
Try it now: Write a one-page staff plan: a 60-minute hands-on training agenda, the rules teachers must follow, the support they will get, and the notes you will ask them to keep.
You can now prepare and support staff for an AI pilot.

check.q: What should staff support during the pilot include?
options: A named contact and weekly check-ins
A one-time email
An AI chatbot only
Nothing; teachers figure it out
check.why: Named support and regular check-ins keep problems from growing.

check.q: Teachers ask why they must keep notes during the pilot. What would you say?
options: It is a rule from the vendor
It is to judge their teaching
Their notes are part of the evidence for deciding what happens next
It is optional busywork
check.why: Teacher notes are evidence for the go, adjust or stop decision.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Communicating with families
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a family letter and FAQ that explain the pilot honestly.
This lesson builds toward: For families of students in the pilot, you will write an honest family letter and a five-question FAQ, under one page, checked by a parent or family liaison, with translations checked by qualified speakers.
Families trust what they understand. Tell them before the pilot starts: what problem you are working on, what the AI tool does, what it does not do (it does not make grades or placement decisions), what student data is used and how it is protected, and who to contact with questions.
Add a short FAQ: Will my child's data be used to train AI? (Answer from your vendor agreement.) Can my child opt out, and what is the alternative? How will you know if it is working? The FTC suggests schools tell parents which online services they have approved; FERPA gives parents the right to inspect their child's education records.
Write in plain English and provide translations checked by qualified speakers for families who need them. Offer a short information session or a time to ask questions.
Step by step:
- Explain the problem and what the tool does and does not do.
- Explain data use and protection.
- Add an FAQ: training, opt-out, measures.
- Translate, with checks by qualified speakers.
- Offer a time for questions.
Words to know:
- FAQ: frequently asked questions: a short list of common questions with answers.
- Opt out: choosing not to take part.
Official sources:
- FTC: Complying with COPPA, Frequently Asked Questions
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy
Try it now: Write the family letter (under one page) and a five-question FAQ for your pilot. Ask a parent or a family liaison to read it and tell you what is unclear.
You can now explain an AI pilot to families clearly and honestly.

check.q: What should the family letter say the tool does NOT do?
options: Help students practice
Make grades or placement decisions
Run on school computers
Use the internet
check.why: Families need to know that people, not AI, make decisions about their children.

check.q: A family liaison says your letter is hard to understand. What would you do?
options: Send it anyway
Add more detail and legal terms
Send it only in English
Rewrite it in plain words and ask them to read it again
check.why: The letter only works if families can understand it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring success and presenting your plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set measures and a decision rule, and present the plan in ten minutes.
This lesson builds toward: For your full pilot plan, you will set three to five success measures with a baseline and a go, adjust or stop rule, and present the plan, in ten minutes, with the rule written before the start and the questions and answers recorded.
Pick three to five measures that match your problem, with a baseline from before the pilot: a student outcome (unit test results, practice completed), a teacher measure (time saved, confidence), a student or family experience measure (a short survey), and a safety measure (incidents, privacy issues). Report results by student group where privacy allows, to catch unequal effects.
Write the decision rule in advance: go (expand), adjust (change and re-test) or stop. For example: "Expand if test results improve and teachers save time, with no serious incidents and no group doing worse."
Present in ten minutes: the problem and evidence, the pilot and tool, the privacy and equity check, the people plan, the measures and the decision rule. Invite hard questions; they make the plan stronger.
Step by step:
- Choose 3-5 measures: student, teacher, experience, safety.
- Collect a baseline.
- Plan to look at results by group where privacy allows.
- Write the go, adjust or stop rule.
- Present in ten minutes and record the questions.
Words to know:
- Measure: something you count or rate to see if a change worked.
- Decision rule: a rule written in advance for whether to expand, adjust or stop.
Try it now: Final task: assemble your full pilot plan (problem, scope and tool, privacy and equity check, staff plan, family letter and FAQ, measures with baseline, decision rule), present it in ten minutes to a leadership team, colleague group or board, and record the questions and your answers.
You can now design, defend and lead a responsible AI pilot in your school or district.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem and evidence Starts from a tool, or has no evidence. States the problem and who it serves, with evidence. Explains why AI is the right answer, or what else was considered. Scope and tool No clear who, what or how long, or the tool has no vendor review. Pilot scope (who, what, how long) and the tool, with its vendor review. The scope is small enough to run in six to twelve weeks. Privacy and equity check FERPA, COPPA (if under 13), accessibility or access is missing. Covers FERPA, COPPA if under 13, accessibility and access. Each risk has a guard and an owner, and the privacy officer has reviewed it. Staff and families No staff-training plan, or no family letter and FAQ. A staff-training plan, and a family letter with a short FAQ. The letter was read by a parent or family liaison and improved. Measures and decision rule Fewer than three measures, no baseline, or no decision rule. Three to five success measures with a baseline, and a go, adjust or stop rule. Includes a safety measure and a plan to look at results by student group. Presentation Not presented, or questions not recorded. Presented in ten minutes, with the questions and answers recorded. Hard questions were welcomed and answered from the plan's evidence. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Before the pilot
Halfway through the pilot
After the pilot ends
Only if the pilot fails
check.why: A baseline before the pilot shows whether anything changed.

check.q: Results look good overall, but one student group did worse. What does your plan do?
options: Report only the overall result
Go ahead, since most students did well
Look at results by group and choose adjust or stop as the decision rule says
Remove that group from the data
check.why: Looking by group catches unequal effects, and the decision rule guides what to do.
